Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bartender
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Leila was eight years old the first time she saw her father’s hand move that way—fast, flat, and final—across her mother’s face. She remembers the crack of impact and the way her mother’s body folded sideways, but if anyone asks her what happened, the words disappear. The memory is all heat and pressure behind her eyes, a chest that locks, a throat that closes. She cannot narrate it. She can only feel it, fresh and suffocating, as if no time has passed.

Now thirty, Leila works behind a bar in a downtown lounge. The job demands constant motion—shaking cocktails, reaching for bottles, wiping counters—and constant exposure to people. That is where the trouble lives. A customer reaches suddenly for a napkin and Leila’s body locks. Shoulders rise, breath stops. She sees the movement before she registers the intention, and everything in her screams that something bad is about to happen. She has learned to fade backward, to keep the bar between herself and anyone who gestures too quickly. It feels less like a choice than a reflex, a muscle memory she never asked for.

She has also learned to prepare. Before every shift, she runs the worst outcomes through her mind: a drunk man grabs her wrist, a fight breaks out, the door won’t lock. She rehearses her response—what she would say, where she would run, how she would protect herself—so that nothing ever catches her off guard. The rehearsal helps, but it also exhausts her. She is always two steps ahead, and the cost of staying ready is that she is never really present.

At home, Leila checks the front door three times before she can sit down. She checks the windows. She checks them again before she lies down. She knows it is excessive—she lives on the third floor, the locks are new—but the ritual quiets something in her chest, so she does it. She has come to believe that safety exists only in a very short list of places: her apartment, the back corner of the bar near the exit, her car with all doors locked. Anywhere else feels too exposed. Open spaces especially—parking lots, wide sidewalks, the dining room of a restaurant—make her feel as though she is being watched from every angle. She avoids them.

She avoids a lot, actually. She avoids emotional conversations because she learned long ago that feelings lead to scenes, and scenes lead to harm. She keeps her voice flat at work. She does not date. She does not let herself get angry, because she is not sure she could stop it if she started. She has come to doubt every decision she makes, second-guessing whether she locked the door right, whether she read a customer’s mood correctly, whether she should have stayed home. She tells herself she cannot rely on herself. She tells herself people cannot be trusted, and the world has proved her right.

Her marriage ended two years ago. Her ex-husband was not abusive—he was patient, even kind—but Leila could not stop scanning his movements, could not shake the certainty that he would one day raise his hand. She checked the locks when he was home. She rehearsed what she would do if he turned. He asked her why she flinched when he touched her shoulder, and she could not explain. She had no words. They parted with a quiet divorce, and she told herself it was for the best.

What finally brought her into the clinic was an incident two weeks ago. A man at the bar lunged for a falling glass. Leila saw the lunge and dropped to the floor, covered her head, and did not come up until a coworker touched her arm. She was humiliated. She was terrified. The manager asked if she needed to go home. She said no, finished her shift, but the shaking did not stop. That night she could not sleep. She checked the locks fourteen times. She rehearsed what she would do if the bar was robbed, if she was attacked on the street, if she lost her job because she could not hold herself together.

Now she sits in the therapist’s office with her hands folded in her lap. She does not know how to say what happened to her as a child. She does not know if saying it will make it worse. But she knows she cannot keep living this way—split between a past she cannot speak and a present she cannot trust. She is afraid that she will never feel safe, and afraid that asking for help is just another thing she will do wrong. But she is here. That, at least, is something.
